root.name: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit Accepted
root.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3

sources.title: Smith-Morra Gambit Guide: How to Play It & Beat It
Smith-Morra Gambit searches (chess.com history, TheChessWorld, Siberian Trap pages; snippet only)

overview: After 3...dxc3 White offers a pawn and recaptures 4.Nxc3, leaving White a piece up in development and a pawn down, with half-open c- and d-files. The aim is Nf3, Bc4 (hitting f7), O-O, Qe2, Rd1 and Rac1, with thematic Nd5 or e5 breaks and sometimes sacrifices on d5. Black develops with ...Nc6, ...e6 and ...d6 (Scheveningen-like set-ups with ...Nf6 and ...Be7, the Siberian ...Ng4, the Chicago ...a6/...b5), takes care of the king on the c4-g8 diagonal, and may return the pawn if needed. Sources describe it as objectively around equal or slightly favouring Black with best play but a serious practical weapon, especially below top level; many Sicilian players avoid it by declining with 3...Nf6 (Alapin-type) or 3...d3. Little theory is needed on White's side, but Black has to know specific defensive set-ups and traps such as the Siberian Trap.

white_ideas.idea: Develop rapidly with Nc3, Nf3, Bc4, castle, then Qe2, Rd1 and Rac1 to pressure the c- and d-files.
Bishop on c4 aiming at f7 and the dark squares, forcing Black to solve king-safety problems before consolidating the extra pawn.
Thematic Nd5 jumps, knight or bishop sacrifices on d5, and the e5 break when Black lags in development (Esserman's 'Mayhem in the Morra' line with Nd5).

black_ideas.idea: Finish development and reduce the force of the c4 bishop; hold the extra pawn if possible, or return material to neutralise the initiative.
Set-ups with ...Nc6, ...e6, ...d6, ...Nf6, ...Be7 (Scheveningen formation), or ...Nc6 with ...e6 and ...Nge7; control e5 and avoid early king exposure.
Siberian Variation with ...Ng4 and its trap (9.h3?? Nd4! wins the queen), and Chicago set-up with ...a6 and ...b5.
If Black consolidates and keeps the pawn, the extra pawn gives good chances in the endgame.

typical_structures.structure: Open game with half-open c- and d-files: White has an e4 pawn and developed pieces, Black has an extra pawn (a Scheveningen-like d6/e6 formation).
Piece play on the c4-g8 diagonal and c-file instead of a pawn centre; White's compensation is activity rather than space.

character.notes: Initiative and direct attack: rapid development, open lines, tactical pressure, queen traps (Siberian). Black can steer to quiet play by returning the pawn, but the standard play is concrete and double-edged with a risk of Black collapsing quickly on the c4-g8 diagonal.

gambit.notes: After 3...dxc3 White is a pawn down. Black may keep it: sources say good endgame chances follow if Black consolidates, and White has no forced win of the pawn back. White's compensation is activity.

soundness.notes: Not refuted; 'sound enough to be a serious practical weapon, especially below top elite level', though Black may equalise with best preparation. Chess Doctrine: objectively close to equal with best play; statistics quoted as 26% White wins, 36% draws, 38% Black wins (source does not say which games). Played occasionally by Nakamura (against Caruana, 2023 rapid) and Nepomniachtchi.

structure.notes: Open lines with half-open c- and d-files and piece activity; typical play does not close the centre. The c-pawn is gone, the d-pawn is gone, and e4 versus Black's d6/e6 pawns forms a Scheveningen-like set-up.

approach.notes: A specific gambit against the Sicilian, not a set-up played against anything. 'Popular at the club level and played occasionally by masters'; 'less commonly seen at the highest levels'. Esserman wrote a book on it; Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi have used it. Many Sicilian players decline with 3...Nf6.

level.notes: Chessworld: minimal theory load for White; 'ideas before memorizing sidelines', six to ten model games enough. Chess Doctrine: White's plans are straightforward, Black needs memorisation of specific defensive set-ups. For the side that studies the line (White), few lines but tactical hazards (Siberian Trap, Nd5 sacrifices).

plan_phrases: pressure on the c- and d-files

sublines_that_differ.name: Siberian Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Nxc3 e6 5. Nf3 Nc6 6. Bc4 Nf6 7. O-O Qc7
sublines_that_differ.how: Black sets a queen trap with ...Ng4 and ...Nd4 (9.h3?? Nd4!); sharper and trickier than the Scheveningen set-ups.

sublines_that_differ.name: Chicago Defense
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Nxc3 Nc6 5. Nf3 ... a6 and ...b5
sublines_that_differ.how: Black expands on the queenside with ...a6 and ...b5 to drive away the bishop.

sublines_that_differ.name: Scheveningen Formation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Nxc3 Nc6 5. Nf3 d6 6. Bc4 e6
sublines_that_differ.how: Quiet, solid Black set-up behind d6 and e6 with ...Nf6 and ...Be7; White keeps the initiative with rapid development.

description.claim: The Smith-Morra Gambit is a sharp and aggressive response to the Sicilian where White sacrifices a pawn to accelerate development and seize the initiative.
description.note: Pawn offered for rapid development and open lines.

description.claim: By opening the c and d-files, White aims for a swift attack, putting immediate pressure on Black's position.
description.note: Pressure on the c- and d-files is the stated compensation.

description.claim: It is perfect for tactical players who thrive on the initiative and are comfortable with a material deficit.
description.note: Sources call it a practical weapon and note it scores well through initiative and tactical pressure, especially below the top level.

common_plans.claim: White: develop pieces rapidly (Nc3, Nf3, Bc4, Bg5/f4) to control the centre and open files, pressuring Black's queen and f7.
common_plans.note: Nc3, Nf3, Bc4, and f7 pressure are named; Bg5/f4 are not named in the sources read.

common_plans.claim: White: launch a direct attack against the Black king, often with further sacrifices.
common_plans.note: Sacrifices on d5 (knight or bishop) and attack on the king's diagonal are named.

common_plans.claim: Black: consolidate the extra pawn and complete development safely, often adopting a hedgehog-like set-up.
common_plans.note: Consolidation and safe development are named, but the usual set-ups are Scheveningen-style (...d6, ...e6, ...Nf6, ...Be7), the Siberian and the Chicago, not a hedgehog (own understanding, unsourced: a hedgehog has pawns on a6, b6, d6, e6).

common_plans.claim: Black: neutralise White's initiative with piece exchanges and use the material advantage in the endgame.
common_plans.note: Wikipedia says Black has good endgame chances if the extra pawn is kept; returning material is a recognised alternative.
